section_summaries.epidemiology: Anisakidosis is most prevalent in Japan (over 90% of cases), with other cases reported in Korea, Europe (Netherlands, Spain, Italy, Germany, France), and increasingly in the United States, Canada, Brazil, Chile, Egypt, and New Zealand. Infection occurs after consuming raw, marinated, or incompletely cooked marine fish or squid. Coastal populations and men aged 20-50 years in Japan are more frequently affected. Risk is higher with less expensive fish like cod, herring, and mackerel, and lower in sushi served by expert chefs. Specific fish species responsible include mackerel and squid in Japan, herring in the Netherlands, Pacific salmon in the US, and pickled anchovies in Spain. Pseudoterranovosis, mainly transmitted by cod, Pacific halibut, wild salmon, and red snapper, is more common in the United States and Canada. Prevalence varies by season and fish size.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Adult anisakid worms reside in the stomachs or intestines of marine mammals (primary hosts). Eggs pass in feces, embryonate in seawater, and develop into L2 larvae. Crustaceans (intermediate hosts) ingest L2 larvae, which mature into L3 larvae. Infected crustaceans are eaten by marine fish or squid (second intermediate hosts), where L3 larvae migrate into viscera, peritoneal cavity, and musculature. Marine mammals become infected by eating uncooked fish/squid, leading to development into adult worms. Humans are accidental hosts who ingest raw or undercooked infected fish/squid, causing larvae to embed in gastric or intestinal mucosa, leading to a hypersensitivity reaction characterized by a granulomatous, eosinophilic infiltrate.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: There are four main clinical syndromes: gastric, intestinal, ectopic (extra-gastrointestinal), and allergic anisakidosis. P. decipiens infections typically involve the stomach and are milder, sometimes presenting as a worm coughed up with a 'tingling throat syndrome'. Gastric anisakidosis, caused by Anisakis spp., presents with severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever 1-12 hours post-ingestion; it can lead to ulcer-like symptoms. Intestinal anisakidosis manifests with intermittent or constant abdominal pain 5-7 days (or longer) post-exposure, primarily in the terminal ileum, and can lead to complications like obstruction or perforation. Ectopic anisakiasis results from rare larval penetration and migration to peritoneal, pleural, mesenteric, hepatic, pancreatic, ovarian, or subcutaneous tissues. Allergic anisakidosis develops 1-24 hours post-ingestion, ranging from respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal pain, urticaria, and angioedema to anaphylaxis, often accompanied by high and persistent IgE levels to A. simplex.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on a patient's food history, especially in cases of acute abdominal pain. Definitive diagnosis is made by examining larvae after endoscopic or surgical removal. Endoscopy can reveal the worm in the gastric mucosa, along with erythema, edema, erosions, tumor-like nodules, or thickened gastric folds. Gastric anisakidosis may be mistaken for peptic ulcers, gastritis, or carcinoma. Intestinal infections have a broad differential diagnosis due to non-specific symptoms. Serological tests like enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for anti-A. simplex IgE can aid diagnosis when clinical findings are inconclusive. Allergic anisakidosis diagnosis includes a history of allergic reactions after fish consumption/exposure, positive skin-prick test, elevated anti-A. simplex IgE, and absence of reaction to fish proteins. Molecular methods (multiplex PCR) can identify nematodes in fish and human isolates.
section_summaries.treatment: For gastric anisakidosis, endoscopic extraction of the larva is the preferred treatment, unless the worm is spontaneously regurgitated. Surgical removal may be necessary for intestinal or extra-intestinal infections, especially if complications like intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, or peritonitis occur. For intestinal anisakidosis without invasive procedures, supportive therapy often leads to clinical resolution. Albendazole (400 mg daily or twice daily for 6-21 days) has limited evidence of effectiveness in humans, performing poorly in a rat model.
section_summaries.prevention: Preventive measures include avoiding the consumption of raw, inadequately cooked, marinated, or salted marine fish, squid, and potentially clams. Reducing risk also involves examining fish for parasites, extracting visible parasites, and removing heavily parasitized fish. Eviscerating fish as soon as possible prevents larval migration from the intestinal tract into edible muscle. Effective cooking methods and proper freezing techniques (e.g., -20°C for 7 days, or blast freezing to -35°C for 15 hours or longer) are crucial for prevention.
